entries.agent_impact: Facts about the lifecycle journal, however the journal was selected (--lifecycle-journal, CAMPAIGNS_OS_LIFECYCLE_LOG, or an active run session). A known command run with --no-write no longer appends an entry. A refused invocation — an unknown command, an unknown subcommand refused before its handler runs, or a flag the command refuses up front — never appends one and creates no file of its own, with or without --no-write. A command that fails inside its handler still appends; `next <unknown-stage>` is such a failure, because it resolves the workspace before it rejects the stage. `run status` never appends one, with or without --no-write. One effect still precedes argument refusal: `start`, `prepare-build`, `build`, `run start` and `run end` close out a stale run session at the root they are about to act on (Run Record assembled and remitted under the usual consent, session file cleared) before argv is refused — a declared effect of those commands, now suppressed by --no-write, which therefore leaves the target byte-identical. A workflow that needs a journal entry for an inspection must run a known command without --no-write; removing --no-write from a refused invocation or from `run status` will not produce one. A workflow that relied on `run end --no-write` reporting a stale closeout gets "no active run session to end" instead: --no-write no longer performs the closeout it could not record.

changes.summary: --no-write writes nothing: it suppresses the lifecycle-journal append for every command and the pre-dispatch stale-session closeout that start/prepare-build/build/run start/run end perform. entries.agent_impact: A new supported CLI command, `campaigns-os readback <target-repo-root> [--json]`, projects a read-only view of a run's emitted artifacts and writes nothing under the target (no lifecycle journal entry either). Its JSON payload is the new `campaigns-os-readback/v2` contract: staleness is assessed per artifact, so `staleness.stale` is true when ANY loaded artifact predates the checkout's last HEAD movement, where the previous projection compared only the newest artifact and reported such a set fresh. A consumer gating on freshness should accept `campaigns-os-readback/v2` and read `staleness.stale_keys` or `staleness.artifacts` to name the stale artifacts. An artifact that recorded a `generated_at` the readback cannot parse has an age it never established: `staleness.unparseable_keys` names those artifacts in render order, their artifact rows carry the shape of the refused value rather than the value, and `clean` is false whenever that list is non-empty, so an unknown age can no longer ride along on a fresh sibling. `computable` and `stale` keep their meanings, and an artifact carrying no `generated_at` key at all is unchanged — it recorded no age to check, so it stays out of the comparison and is not by itself unclean. Separately, the four mutating commands that lacked one gain `--dry-run`: `run-record`, `qa publish`, `checkpoint waive` and `theme waive`. Each validates and assembles exactly as the real command does, writes nothing under the target and opens no connection, and exits as the real command would — so an agent can preview a Run Record, a verdict publish or a waiver before committing to it. Validation is not weaker under the flag: every check on the route from argv to the first effect runs, by the same code, including the ones that live inside the effect — an invalid Run Record is refused with the writer's own message and exit 1, a waive over a report that is not an Assembly Report object is refused as the commit refuses it, and a `--proxy-base` the transport declines before it opens a socket fails `qa publish --dry-run` with `publish_failed` and exit 1 exactly as the real publish does. The envelopes gain `dry_run: true` plus `would_write`/`would_remit` and `would_remit_refused` (run-record), `would_publish`/`would_post` with `status: "dry_run"` (qa publish), and `would_write` with `status: "dry_run"` (both waives); `run end` carries the flag through and leaves the session open. On those commands a `--dry-run` invocation also appends no command-lifecycle entry and runs no stale-session closeout, so an idle session is left on disk for a real invocation and `run end --dry-run` at a root whose only session is stale refuses with `No active run session to end`; on a command that does not implement the flag (`qa run`, say) the shared parser still accepts it and the command behaves exactly as before, lifecycle entry included. No existing command, flag or output changed.
